title: Billing platforms for AI and LLM token-based pricing
summary: Compare Metronome, Orb, and the existing Stripe Billing Meters path for AI usage billing. Evaluate credits, rate changes, contracts, and invoice reconciliation.
body_markdown:
For AI usage billing, choose a platform based on the billing rules you need to prove: how it counts usage, applies prices, spends credits, corrects mistakes, and produces an invoice your customer can check.


Metronome and Orb are options to evaluate for usage-heavy products. If you already use Stripe Billing Meters, assess that integration against your needs before changing it. Stripe's current documentation directs new usage-based billing builds to Metronome.


This comparison uses the vendors' public documentation reviewed on September 24, 2026. It does not claim hands-on performance results or rank vendors by unverified prices.


## Which platform should you evaluate?


Option Documented scope Start here when What to prove in a trial


Metronome Usage pricing, prepaid credits, recurring fees, and negotiated commitments Your product combines self-serve usage with enterprise contracts Credit consumption, amendments, access controls, and the full invoice flow


Orb Usage, seat, and hybrid pricing; query-based metrics; credits; pricing simulations Your team needs to test rates against usage and revise billing data Correction behavior, metric ownership, credit rules, and exports


Existing Stripe Billing Meters integration Meter events and metered subscription billing You already run this setup and need to assess whether it still fits Processing delay, credit constraints, late usage, and migration cost


Sources:[Metronome documentation](https://docs.metronome.com/guides/get-started/home) ,[Orb documentation](https://docs.withorb.com/overview) , and[Stripe's usage-recording guidance](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/recording-usage) .


These are evaluation paths, not a claim that one product is best for every AI company.


## Metronome: Evaluate complex usage and contract terms


Metronome documents pay-as-you-go billing, subscriptions with usage, prepaid credits, and enterprise commitments. Its enterprise model includes negotiated discounts and contract renewals.


This makes it worth evaluating when a single product needs both a small self-serve plan and a negotiated enterprise deal. In the trial, use your actual contract terms. A simple token counter will not expose problems with shared commitments, midterm changes, or credit expiry.


Confirm how the platform connects to payment collection, tax, and your ledger. A rating result is only one part of the billing process.


## Orb: Evaluate query-based metrics and pricing changes


Orb documents custom SQL metrics, usage and seat pricing, prepaid credits, and simulations using historical usage. It also documents backfills and amendments.


Evaluate that model if your team wants to define billable usage from event data and test a price change before applying it. Ask who owns each metric and how a change gets reviewed. A flexible query can still bill the wrong event if the definition is wrong.


Prove what happens to draft and finalized invoices when you correct historical usage. Check the customer-visible adjustment and the accounting export, not just the revised total.


## Stripe Billing Meters: Review the path for an existing setup


Stripe's current[recording usage page](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/recording-usage) describes Billing Meters for existing integrations and recommends Metronome for new builds. Do not start a new design from an old tutorial without checking that guidance.


If you already use Billing Meters, assess whether the current flow meets your product's needs. Stripe processes meter events asynchronously, so your application should not treat an invoice meter as an instant access limit.


A migration has costs too: customer IDs, price history, credits, open invoices, and reconciliations all need a plan. Move only after you can reproduce the old system's valid results and explain intended differences.


## What to test for token-based pricing


Keep input, output, cached usage, and other billable units separate when your contract gives them different prices. Preserve the model and price version on each event.


Ask the platform to calculate a sample month that includes:


- A request delivered twice to the ingestion endpoint.
- A failed provider call and a retry.
- A model or price change during the month.
- An event that arrives after the billing period closes.
- Paid credits and promotional credits.
- An enterprise minimum plus usage above that minimum.
- A refund after an invoice has been paid.


Compare the result with a calculation your team can check independently. Use[credits vs. tokens](https://www.afternoon.co/blog/ai-credits-vs-tokens) to define the customer unit before testing.


## What should you use for volume-priced data API calls?


First define whether you mean **volume** pricing, where the selected rate applies to all units, or **graduated** pricing, where each band has its own rate.


Then choose the billable event: all requests, successful requests, records returned, or another defined unit. State how retries and partial results count.


Evaluate a platform using those exact rules and a worked invoice. The[API usage billing guide](https://www.afternoon.co/blog/api-metered-billing-accounting-guide) shows the event-to-invoice process.


## What remains your responsibility?


You still need reliable source events, customer mapping, contract terms, and a way to enforce access. A billing vendor cannot infer whether a failed request should be free.


You also need tax classification and an accounting policy. An invoice total is not automatically recognized revenue. Keep those decisions connected to your[revenue recognition process](https://www.afternoon.co/blog/usage-based-pricing-guide) .


## How to compare cost


Ask each vendor for a quote using the same usage profile, customer count, billing rules, and support needs. Include implementation, payment processing, tax tooling, and ongoing engineering work where they apply.


Do not choose from a headline fee alone. Prefer the option that can reproduce your contracts, explain each charge, and keep that process manageable as the product changes.
